source.title: Williamson–Shmoys · The Design of Approximation Algorithms

problems.title: 0–1 Knapsack
problems.input: Items with nonnegative profits pᵢ, positive weights wᵢ, and a capacity W.
problems.goal: Choose each item at most once, maximizing profit while respecting the capacity.

algorithms.name: Exact Pareto-frontier dynamic programming
algorithms.label: Exact; pseudo-polynomial
algorithms.guarantee: For integer weights and profits, returns an optimum in O(n·min{W,V}) arithmetic operations, where V is total profit. This is not polynomial in binary input length.
steps: Start with the feasible state (weight,profit)=(0,0). Discard items heavier than the capacity.
For each item, merge the old state list with the list obtained by adding that item once to every old state; discard overweight states.
Sort by weight, retain the best profit at each weight, and remove every pair dominated by a no-heavier pair of at least equal profit.
Keep predecessor choices for reconstruction and return the surviving state of greatest profit after all items.
algorithms.proof: Every feasible partial solution is dominated by a retained state. Future item additions preserve dominance. Integer coordinates bound the frontier by min{W+1,V+1}.
algorithms.pitfall: Use the previous item layer when adding an item; updating it in place can accidentally allow the same item repeatedly.

algorithms.name: Profit scaling and profit-indexed dynamic programming
algorithms.label: FPTAS
algorithms.guarantee: For any 0<ε<1, return a feasible set worth at least (1−ε)OPT. The running time is polynomial jointly in input length and 1/ε.
steps: Remove items heavier than W. If no feasible positive-profit item remains, return the empty set. Otherwise let P be the largest remaining profit.
Set K=εP/n and round each profit down to floor(pᵢ/K). Keep the original weights.
For each total scaled profit, compute the minimum attainable original weight. Return a feasible state with maximum scaled profit.
Compare the rounded value of an optimum with the returned value. At most nK≤εOPT is lost; the total scaled-profit range is at most n²/ε.
algorithms.proof: Feasibility stays exact because weights are unchanged. The approximation loss is charged to a computable lower bound P≤OPT.
algorithms.pitfall: A DP polynomial in the numerical capacity W is only pseudo-polynomial when W is binary encoded.

problems.title: Identical-machine makespan scheduling
problems.input: Processing times pⱼ and m identical parallel machines; every job must be assigned to one machine.
problems.goal: Minimize the largest machine load, also called the makespan.

algorithms.name: Enumerate all long-job assignments, then list-schedule
algorithms.label: PTAS for fixed m
algorithms.guarantee: For fixed machine count m, the source’s Aₖ construction returns makespan at most (1+1/k)OPT. It enumerates at most m^(km) long-job placements.
steps: Let P=Σpⱼ and call a job long if pⱼ>P/(km). There are at most km such jobs.
Enumerate every assignment of the long jobs to the m machines and retain one of minimum long-job makespan.
Insert all short jobs on least-loaded machines. Set k≥1/ε for a (1+ε) guarantee with fixed m.
algorithms.proof: A placement agreeing with an optimum on long jobs is enumerated. If a short job determines the final makespan, its start is at most P/m and its length at most P/(km).
algorithms.pitfall: m^(km) is polynomial only when m and the accuracy parameter k are fixed.

algorithms.name: Large-job configurations and size rounding
algorithms.label: PTAS
algorithms.guarantee: For each fixed ε>0, obtain makespan at most (1+ε)OPT in polynomial time. The dependence on 1/ε need not be polynomial.
steps: For a candidate makespan T and accuracy integer k, call a job long when pⱼ>T/k.
Round long jobs downward to multiples of T/k². Enumerate machine configurations of rounded types; each T-load configuration contains at most k long jobs.
Use dynamic programming on type counts to find a rounded placement. Restore original long-job sizes, adding at most T/k per machine.

Insert short jobs on a least-loaded machine. If a short job finishes last, its start is at most the original total processing volume divided by m, hence at most T when T is a valid optimum guess. Search candidate bounds and choose the internal accuracy to obtain the stated PTAS.
algorithms.proof: Long-job restoration and the final short-job bound are two separate cases. Each leads to a T+T/k load bound before the accuracy bookkeeping.
algorithms.pitfall: Do not charge the long-job rounding error a second time in the short-job case.

algorithms.name: Rounded-type feasibility dynamic programming
algorithms.label: Exact rounded-instance solver
algorithms.guarantee: For fixed k, the count-vector DP finds the minimum number of machines for the rounded long jobs with makespan bound T in n^O(k²) time.
steps: After rounding, index the at most k² types by sizes iT/k². Let aᵢ be the number of remaining jobs of type i.
Enumerate nonzero configurations c with Σᵢcᵢ·iT/k²≤T and cᵢ≤aᵢ. A bin contains only boundedly many long jobs.
Use DP(0)=0 and DP(a)=1+min꜀DP(a−c). Store a minimizing configuration for reconstruction.
The rounded instance is feasible on m machines exactly when DP(full counts)≤m.
algorithms.proof: Every machine in an optimum supplies one enumerated configuration; induction on remaining jobs proves the recurrence.
algorithms.pitfall: Feasibility of rounded jobs at T is not feasibility of the original jobs at T.

algorithms.name: Bisection with an approximate-feasibility oracle
algorithms.label: Polynomial search for the PTAS bound
algorithms.guarantee: For integer processing times, bisection around the rounded-type procedure finds an approximate schedule without enumerating every numerical makespan.
steps: Initialize L=max{ceil(Σp/m),max p} and U=ceil(Σp/m)+max p, retaining a schedule from a successful call at U.
While L<U, test T=floor((L+U)/2) using the rounded-long-job procedure, restoring sizes and inserting short jobs on success.
On failure set L=T+1; on success set U=T and retain the actual approximate schedule. Return that retained schedule when L=U.
algorithms.proof: Failure certifies that the original optimum exceeds T, while success returns cost at most (1+ε)T. Only the final actual schedule’s cost is reported.
algorithms.pitfall: Success is not a certificate that the original instance has makespan at most T.

algorithms.name: List scheduling and LPT
algorithms.label: Additional algorithms
algorithms.guarantee: List scheduling gives factor 2−1/m. Sorting jobs by decreasing processing time first (LPT) improves this to 4/3−1/(3m).
steps: List scheduling processes the jobs in a chosen order, always assigning the next job to a least-loaded machine.
LPT uses the same placement rule after sorting jobs by nonincreasing size.
Analyze the last finishing job using the average-workload lower bound and a lower bound from large jobs.
algorithms.proof: The approximation factor depends on the ordering and the lower bound used for the last job.
algorithms.pitfall: These background algorithms solve the same makespan problem; they are not the approximation scheme of §3.2.

problems.title: Bin packing
problems.input: Item sizes sᵢ in (0,1], with an unlimited supply of unit-capacity bins.
problems.goal: Pack every item and minimize the number of bins.

algorithms.name: First-Fit insertion
algorithms.label: At most 2OPT+1 bins
algorithms.guarantee: The elementary analysis in this section gives at most 2OPT+1 bins for arbitrary item order; the same insertion rule extends a packing by small pieces.
steps: Process items in the supplied order, keeping bins in the order in which they were opened.
Put each item in the first existing bin with enough space; open a new bin only if no existing bin can hold it.
For the elementary proof, pair consecutive bins: their combined load exceeds one whenever the second bin was necessary.
algorithms.proof: Total item volume lower-bounds OPT. Pairing used bins bounds their number while leaving the possible final bin explicit.
algorithms.pitfall: Do not identify this elementary bound with the sharper First-Fit-Decreasing result.

algorithms.name: First-Fit-Decreasing
algorithms.label: Cited bound: (11/9)OPT+4
algorithms.guarantee: The assigned text cites the asymptotic bound FFD≤(11/9)OPT+4 and explicitly does not prove it in this section.
steps: Sort all items by nonincreasing size before beginning the packing.
Insert each sorted item into the first previously opened bin with sufficient room.
Open another bin only if all previous bins are too full; retain the source’s additive constant when quoting its bound.
algorithms.proof: Sorting changes the structure of partially filled bins. The sharper analysis is an imported result, not the elementary paired-bin proof.
algorithms.pitfall: Do not claim that the source proves the 11/9 bound here, or silently remove its additive constant.

algorithms.name: Exact configuration DP for a bounded set of large types
algorithms.label: Exact on constant-type instances
algorithms.guarantee: If there are a fixed number of distinct item sizes, each bounded away from zero, the minimum-bin packing can be computed in polynomial time.
steps: Enumerate every feasible single-bin vector of type counts; the lower size bound limits the number of items in a bin.
Use a state for the number of remaining items of each type and set F(0,…,0)=0.
For every state, try a feasible bin configuration and take one plus the best value for the remaining counts; store choices to reconstruct bins.
algorithms.proof: Any optimal packing has a first bin among the enumerated configurations; induction on total item count gives the recurrence.
algorithms.pitfall: The number of types and the maximum items per bin must be bounded for the claimed polynomial running time.

algorithms.name: Extend a large-item packing with small items
algorithms.label: max{ℓ,SIZE/(1−γ)+1} bins
algorithms.guarantee: Starting from ℓ bins holding all items larger than γ, First-Fit inserts the remaining items of size at most γ with the stated additive-bin bound.
steps: Keep the supplied packing of large items and process small items in any order.
Insert each in the first bin that fits it, opening a new bin only when required.
If a new bin opens, every previous bin except the eventual last one has load above 1−γ; charge them to total original volume.
algorithms.proof: Either no bin is added, or fullness of all but the last bin bounds their count by SIZE/(1−γ).
algorithms.pitfall: Using the volume of only the small items loses the existing large-item load from the accounting.

algorithms.name: Linear grouping of large items, then small-item insertion
algorithms.label: Asymptotic PTAS
algorithms.guarantee: After choosing the internal accuracy appropriately, the output uses at most (1+ε)OPT+1 bins. The additive term is part of the guarantee.
steps: Separate large and small items and sort the large items by size.
Partition large items into groups, treating the largest group separately and rounding sizes within later groups upward.
Solve the resulting constant-type large-item packing problem by configuration enumeration and dynamic programming.
Insert small items into available space. When another bin is needed, previously used bins are sufficiently full to bound their number by total item volume.
algorithms.proof: A rounded group can be compared with the larger items in the preceding group. The largest group and the last small-item bin remain visible in the cost accounting.
algorithms.pitfall: An asymptotic guarantee does not imply an absolute (1+ε)-approximation on instances with very few bins.

problems.title: Weighted MAX-SAT
problems.input: Boolean clauses C with nonnegative weights w꜀. Within a clause, normalize repeated or complementary literals as needed.
problems.goal: Find a truth assignment maximizing the weight of satisfied clauses.

algorithms.name: Independent fair truth assignment
algorithms.label: 1/2; 1−2^(−k) for clause length ≥k
algorithms.guarantee: A normalized clause of length ℓ is satisfied with probability 1−2^(−ℓ). Thus general nonempty MAX-SAT has expected ratio 1/2, and exact-length-three clauses give 7/8.
steps: Merge duplicate clauses by adding weights, remove repeated literals, and account for tautologies separately.
Set each remaining variable independently to true with probability one half.
Sum each clause’s satisfaction probability times its weight; compare with total clause weight as an upper bound on OPT.
algorithms.proof: Independence is needed within a clause. Linearity of expectation sums clause contributions without requiring different clauses to be independent.
algorithms.pitfall: The 7/8 claim needs three distinct, noncomplementary literals in each relevant clause.

algorithms.name: Conditional-expectation derandomization
algorithms.label: Deterministic preservation of expectation
algorithms.guarantee: When conditional clause expectations can be computed, the final assignment is at least the expected value of the starting independent distribution; this derandomizes the fair, biased and LP-based methods.
steps: Maintain a partial assignment and the expected weighted satisfaction under independent choices for the unset variables.
Compute this expectation after fixing the next variable to each possible truth value.
Choose the value with the larger conditional expectation and repeat until all variables are fixed.
algorithms.proof: The current expectation is a weighted average of the two conditional expectations. The final expectation is the actual deterministic value.
algorithms.pitfall: An existence proof is not an efficient derandomization unless both conditional expectations are computable.

algorithms.name: Biased coins with unit-clause normalization
algorithms.guarantee: After orienting each variable so its positive unit-clause weight is at least its negative unit-clause weight, independent true probability p=(√5−1)/2 gives expected value at least p·OPT.
steps: For each variable compare the total weights of its positive and negative unit clauses; complement all occurrences if needed to make the positive one heavier.
Set every normalized variable true independently with probability p=(√5−1)/2, which solves p=1−p².
Use the benchmark B=total clause weight minus the smaller unit-clause weight for each variable. Then OPT≤B and the expected value is at least pB.
Undo the variable complementation to return an assignment to the original instance; conditional expectation gives a deterministic version.
algorithms.proof: Every nonnegative unit clause succeeds with probability p, while every longer clause succeeds with probability at least 1−p². Conflicting unit clauses require the improved upper bound B.
algorithms.pitfall: Using one biased coin without normalizing conflicting unit clauses does not justify the 0.618 guarantee.

algorithms.name: Independent LP-marginal rounding
algorithms.label: 1−1/e approximation
algorithms.guarantee: Rounding each truth variable independently with its optimal LP value gives expected satisfaction at least (1−1/e) times the LP optimum, hence at least that fraction of OPT.
steps: Use 0≤yᵢ,z꜀≤1 and impose z꜀≤Σpositive yᵢ+Σnegative(1−yᵢ), maximizing Σw꜀z꜀.
Solve this relaxation and set variable i true independently with probability yᵢ.
Bound a length-ℓ clause’s failure product by AM–GM, then use concavity to obtain satisfaction at least [1−(1−1/ℓ)^ℓ]z꜀.
algorithms.proof: The clause-dependent coefficient is at least 1−1/e. The LP optimum is an upper bound for this maximization problem.
algorithms.pitfall: Independent rounding can leave clauses unsatisfied even when z꜀=1; fractional satisfaction is not literal feasibility.

algorithms.name: Choose the better of fair and LP rounding
algorithms.label: 3/4 approximation
algorithms.guarantee: The expected value of the better of the two complete assignments is at least 3OPT/4. Both distributions can also be derandomized first.
steps: Construct one fair-assignment solution and one independent LP-marginal-rounding solution.
Evaluate their actual total satisfied weights and keep the assignment of greater value.
For each clause length ℓ, average the two lower bounds 1−2^(−ℓ) and 1−(1−1/ℓ)^ℓ; their mean is at least 3/4.
algorithms.proof: max{W₁,W₂}≥(W₁+W₂)/2 pointwise. The improvement comes from complementary clause-length behavior.
algorithms.pitfall: Taking the average of just the global 1/2 and 1−1/e guarantees does not prove 3/4.

algorithms.name: Nonlinear transformed-marginal rounding
algorithms.label: 3/4 approximation
algorithms.guarantee: Choose a computable f with 1−4^(−x)≤f(x)≤4^(x−1) for 0≤x≤1. Setting variable i true independently with probability f(yᵢ) gives expected value at least 3OPT/4.
steps: Solve the same MAX-SAT LP as for marginal rounding.
For an explicit valid transformation use f(x)=1−4^(−x); the inequality 4^x+4^(1−x)≥4 verifies the required upper envelope.
Independently set variable i true with probability f(yᵢ). The failure product of a clause is at most 4^(−z꜀).
Use concavity of 1−4^(−z) on [0,1] to lower-bound satisfaction by 3z꜀/4, then sum weighted clauses.
algorithms.proof: The lower envelope bounds positive-literal failure and the upper envelope bounds negative-literal failure. Both signs must be controlled.
algorithms.pitfall: A transformation that only satisfies the lower bound need not handle negative literals correctly.

problems.title: Weighted MAX-CUT
problems.input: An undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights wᵤᵥ.
problems.goal: Partition vertices into two sides to maximize crossing-edge weight.

algorithms.name: Convert a positive semidefinite Gram matrix to vectors
algorithms.label: Equivalent vector representation
algorithms.guarantee: A positive semidefinite matrix X factors as VᵀV, giving vectors with inner products Xᵢⱼ. Numerical SDP solutions require an explicit precision tolerance.
steps: Express the relaxation using a symmetric matrix X with X≽0, diagonal-one constraints, and the required edge objective or constraints.
Use a spectral or Cholesky-type factorization to obtain V with X=VᵀV; its columns are the required vectors.
Track solver feasibility and objective error through rounding rather than assuming exact real arithmetic or exact polynomial-time solution of every SDP.
algorithms.proof: A Gram matrix is positive semidefinite, and every positive semidefinite matrix admits such a factorization.
algorithms.pitfall: The representation equivalence is not a proof that arbitrary semidefinite programs can be solved exactly in polynomial time.

algorithms.name: Independent random partition
algorithms.label: 1/2 approximation
algorithms.guarantee: Each edge crosses with probability 1/2, so expected cut weight is half of total edge weight and at least half of OPT.
steps: Put each vertex independently on either side with probability 1/2.
For each edge, calculate the probability that its endpoints receive opposite sides.
Sum the weighted contributions; conditional expectation can derandomize this baseline.
algorithms.proof: Every cut uses at most the total nonnegative edge weight.
algorithms.pitfall: A graph may have a maximum cut containing far less than all its edges.

algorithms.name: Greedy conditional-expectation cut
algorithms.label: Deterministic factor 1/2
algorithms.guarantee: With nonnegative edge weights, a sequential choice of sides returns a cut weighing at least half the total edge weight, hence at least OPT/2.
steps: Process vertices in any fixed order, keeping the previous choices unchanged.
For the next vertex, compare its total edge weight to already placed vertices on each side; put it on the opposite side from the larger weight.
Each edge is considered when its later endpoint is placed. Charge at least half of that vertex’s already exposed incident weight to the cut.
algorithms.proof: Every vertex choice maximizes the conditional expectation; edges to unplaced vertices contribute the same expected half-weight under either choice.
algorithms.pitfall: When weights differ, compare weight totals rather than just neighbor counts.

algorithms.name: Goemans–Williamson SDP and hyperplane rounding
algorithms.label: Approximately 0.87856
algorithms.guarantee: With the SDP solution precision accounted for, obtain an expected approximation ratio approximately 0.87856.
steps: Relax binary side labels to unit vectors, represented by a positive semidefinite Gram matrix.
Draw independent standard Gaussian coordinates for a normal vector r; put vertex i on the side given by the sign of vᵢ·r.
An edge of vector angle θ is cut with probability θ/π. Compare this with its SDP contribution (1−cos θ)/2 and sum over edges.
algorithms.proof: Rotational symmetry gives an exact two-dimensional separation probability; the worst angle determines the ratio.
algorithms.pitfall: The edge-wise comparison uses nonnegative weights.

problems.title: Rooted prize-collecting Steiner tree
problems.input: A graph with nonnegative edge costs, a root r, and a nonnegative penalty πᵥ for each vertex.
problems.goal: Choose a tree containing r, paying for its edges and for every excluded vertex.

algorithms.name: Random threshold rounding
algorithms.label: Expected factor approximately 2.542
algorithms.guarantee: The threshold distribution balances the expected connection cost and the expected omitted-vertex penalty, giving factor 1/(1−e⁻¹ᐟ²).
steps: Solve the cut-based LP with fractional edge variables and fractional vertex-inclusion variables.
Sample a threshold α uniformly from [e⁻¹ᐟ²,1] and retain vertices whose inclusion value is at least α.
Connect retained vertices using the tree-rounding guarantee that bounds connection cost by 2/α times the fractional edge cost.
Integrate that connection bound and the exclusion probabilities over α. The lower endpoint makes the two coefficients equal.
algorithms.proof: The integral of 1/α controls connection cost, while a vertex’s exclusion probability controls its penalty.
algorithms.pitfall: Substituting the mean threshold into 1/α does not compute its expectation.

problems.title: Metric uncapacitated facility location
problems.input: Potential facilities with opening costs, clients, and connection costs induced by a metric.
problems.goal: Open facilities and assign every client to one of them, minimizing opening plus assignment cost. Facilities have no capacity limit.

algorithms.name: Cluster clients before randomized facility selection
algorithms.label: Expected factor 3
algorithms.guarantee: The assigned clustering-and-rounding algorithm is a randomized 3-approximation under the metric assumption.
steps: Solve the facility-location primal and dual LPs. Let N(j)={i:xᵢⱼ>0}, N²(j) be clients sharing a neighbor, and Cⱼ=Σᵢcᵢⱼxᵢⱼ.
Among unassigned clients choose j minimizing the dual value vⱼ plus Cⱼ.
Open exactly one facility i in N(j), sampled with probabilities xᵢⱼ. Assign j and all still-unassigned clients in N²(j) to i.
Remove those clients and repeat. Disjoint representative neighborhoods bound opening costs; dual feasibility and the metric inequality bound reassignment.
algorithms.proof: Controlled opening marginals bound facility cost; triangle inequalities bound rerouting cost.
algorithms.pitfall: Independent facility openings alone can leave an entire client support closed.

problems.title: Single-machine weighted completion time with release dates
problems.input: Jobs with processing times pⱼ>0, release dates rⱼ≥0, and weights wⱼ≥0.
problems.goal: Schedule jobs nonpreemptively on one machine, start each no earlier than its release date, and minimize weighted completion time.
problems.objective: \min\sum_j w_jC_j\quad\text{with}\quad S_j\ge r_j\quad\text{and nonoverlapping job intervals}.

algorithms.name: Event-based preemptive density-priority relaxation
algorithms.label: Exact relaxation subroutine
algorithms.guarantee: For integer processing times, release dates and weights, this computes an optimum of the section’s midpoint-objective relaxation in polynomial time; it is not an optimum nonpreemptive schedule.
steps: Sort jobs by nonincreasing density wⱼ/pⱼ and maintain their remaining processing times.
At each release or completion event, run the highest-density available unfinished job, preempting if a denser job becomes available.
Represent processing by the at most 2n event intervals rather than enumerating every time slot.
For each job, compute its average processing-time midpoint plus pⱼ/2 from these intervals, obtaining Cⱼ for the relaxation objective.
algorithms.proof: An interchange argument puts higher-density available work first for the linear time-price objective. The relaxation underestimates every feasible nonpreemptive schedule.
algorithms.pitfall: Shortest remaining processing time is a different priority rule; do not replace the fixed density order.

algorithms.name: Randomized α-point ordering
algorithms.label: Expected factor 2
algorithms.guarantee: The resulting feasible nonpreemptive schedule has expected weighted completion cost at most twice OPT.
steps: Compute a fractional/preemptive scheduling relaxation that lower-bounds the nonpreemptive objective.
Choose an independent uniform αⱼ in [0,1] for each job; use the time by which αⱼ of its fractional processing is complete as its ordering point.
Order jobs by these points and process them nonpreemptively, waiting when needed to respect release dates.
Condition on one job’s point, bound earlier workload and release-date delay using fractional prefix capacities, then average and sum with weights.
algorithms.proof: The fractional schedule’s capacity constraints bound expected work placed before a job.
algorithms.pitfall: A raw time-indexed formulation with a binary-encoded huge horizon is not automatically a polynomial implementation.

algorithms.name: One common α and deterministic enumeration
algorithms.label: Randomized and deterministic factor 2
algorithms.guarantee: The source states that one uniform α shared by all jobs also gives expected factor 2, and that enumerating the at most n resulting schedules derandomizes it. Its shared-α proof is explicitly outside the section.
steps: Use the same density-priority preemptive schedule and choose one α uniformly in [0,1] for all jobs.
Order jobs by their α-points and run the resulting nonpreemptive schedule as early as release dates permit.
For derandomization enumerate the distinct orderings obtained as α crosses the breakpoints of the event schedule, evaluate their weighted completion costs, and take the best.
algorithms.proof: Only finitely many schedules occur, so one attains at most the expected cost. The expectation guarantee here is an imported source result, not the independent-points proof.
algorithms.pitfall: Independence of per-job αⱼ is unavailable for the common-α variant; it needs its own analysis.

problems.title: Minimum-congestion integer multicommodity routing
problems.input: An undirected graph and source–sink pairs (sᵢ,tᵢ), each requiring one path.
problems.goal: Choose a simple path for every pair, minimizing the maximum number of selected paths sharing an edge.

algorithms.name: Independent path rounding and Chernoff analysis
algorithms.label: High-probability congestion bounds
algorithms.guarantee: For LP value W*≥c ln n, congestion is at most W*+√(cW* ln n) with high probability for a suitable constant c. The general bound is O(log n)·max{W*,1}; Exercise 5.13 sharpens the logarithmic factor.
algorithms.tex: W_{\rm out}\le W^*+\sqrt{cW^*\ln n}\quad\text{when }W^*\ge c\ln n.
steps: Relax each pair’s path choice to a probability distribution, minimizing fractional maximum edge load W*.
Independently choose exactly one path for each pair from that pair’s distribution.
For a fixed edge, express load as a sum of independent indicators over pairs and apply a Chernoff bound.
Union-bound the edge failures. For a nontrivial instance, max{W*,1} is also a lower bound on the integral optimum.
algorithms.proof: Independence is across different pairs for one fixed edge. Loads on different edges need not be independent.
algorithms.pitfall: The additive square-root bound needs the stated large-W* condition; it is not unconditional.

algorithms.name: Compact edge-flow LP and path decomposition
algorithms.label: Equivalent fractional relaxation
algorithms.guarantee: A polynomial-sized multicommodity edge-flow LP realizes the path relaxation’s value; a polynomial number of flow paths suffice for independent path rounding.
steps: For each commodity and each directed orientation of an undirected edge introduce nonnegative flow, impose unit source-to-sink conservation, and bound total bidirectional load on each edge by W.
Solve the LP minimizing W, then cancel cycles in each commodity without increasing any edge load.
Repeatedly extract a positive-flow source-to-sink path, subtract its minimum edge flow, and record that mass as its sampling probability.
algorithms.proof: Flow conservation permits path decomposition, and each extraction removes at least one positive edge. Cycle removal never increases congestion.
algorithms.pitfall: Sample one complete path per commodity; independently rounding individual edge flows can disconnect the route.

problems.title: Proper 3-coloring of dense 3-colorable graphs
problems.input: A graph promised to be 3-colorable, with every vertex having at least δn neighbors for a fixed δ>0.
problems.goal: Find a proper coloring using at most three colors.

algorithms.name: Sample, enumerate, and solve a 2-SAT extension
algorithms.label: Exact 3-coloring with high probability
algorithms.guarantee: For fixed δ, the randomized algorithm runs in polynomial time and finds a proper 3-coloring with high probability.
steps: Sample O(log n/δ) vertices so that, with high probability, every vertex outside the sample has a sampled neighbor.
Enumerate the sample’s possible 3-colorings. Its logarithmic size makes this polynomial for fixed δ.
A sampled neighbor excludes one color at an outside vertex, leaving at most two choices.
Encode the remaining edge restrictions as 2-SAT. The enumeration containing a restriction of a genuine coloring has a satisfying extension.
algorithms.proof: The minimum-degree assumption makes a small random sample dominate all remaining vertices.
algorithms.pitfall: A constant total edge density does not by itself imply the required minimum-degree promise.

algorithms.name: Extend two-color lists using the implication graph
algorithms.label: Exact extension or rejection
algorithms.guarantee: Once a sampled coloring leaves at most two possible colors at every remaining vertex, a 2-SAT instance decides exactly whether that sampled coloring extends.
steps: Remove neighbor colors fixed by the sample. Reject an empty color list and force any singleton choice.
Give a binary variable to each two-color list. For every edge, forbid each pair of choices giving its endpoints the same color by a clause (¬choiceᵤ∨¬choiceᵥ).
For each clause a∨b add implication edges ¬a→b and ¬b→a. Compute strongly connected components.
Reject if a variable and its negation share a component; otherwise use reverse topological component order to obtain a satisfying choice and verify the coloring.
algorithms.proof: Every forbidden local color collision is encoded as a clause, and the SCC criterion is exact for 2-SAT.
algorithms.pitfall: Dense sampling and this extension solver are separate steps: 2-SAT alone does not solve unrestricted 3-coloring.

problems.title: Coloring general 3-colorable graphs with few colors
problems.input: A graph promised to be 3-colorable, without a minimum-degree assumption.
problems.goal: Produce a proper coloring whose number of colors is provably controlled as a function of n or maximum degree Δ.
problems.objective: \text{Find a proper }k\text{-coloring, with }k\text{ bounded despite only the promise }\chi(G)\le3.

algorithms.name: High-degree neighborhoods, then greedy coloring
algorithms.label: At most 4√n colors
algorithms.guarantee: For a promised 3-colorable graph, a combinatorial algorithm uses at most 4√n colors; it needs no semidefinite relaxation.
steps: Fix the original n. While some vertex has degree at least √n in the remaining graph, choose one.
Use one fresh color for that vertex and two other fresh colors for its bipartite neighborhood; remove this closed neighborhood.
Greedily color the residual graph, whose maximum degree is below √n, using another palette.
algorithms.proof: The neighbors of a vertex in a 3-colorable graph are bipartite. Each removal eliminates at least √n vertices, so only O(√n) fresh palettes are needed.
algorithms.pitfall: Bipartiteness of every neighborhood uses the 3-colorability promise; it fails for a general graph.

algorithms.name: Two-color a bipartite neighborhood
algorithms.label: Exact two-coloring or conflict detection
algorithms.guarantee: Breadth-first or depth-first traversal two-colors a bipartite graph in linear graph time. A neighborhood of a vertex in a promised 3-colorable graph is bipartite.
steps: Start an unvisited component with one of two colors and explore its edges by BFS or DFS.
Assign every newly reached vertex the opposite color to its parent.
If an edge joins vertices of the same color, report a conflict; otherwise repeat for remaining components.
algorithms.proof: A successful traversal colors every edge properly. A conflict exposes an odd cycle in that component.
algorithms.pitfall: The promise concerns the induced neighborhood; arbitrary graphs need not be two-colorable.

algorithms.name: Greedy coloring of a bounded-degree remainder
algorithms.label: At most Δ+1 colors
algorithms.guarantee: For a graph of maximum degree Δ, sequential greedy coloring always returns a proper coloring using at most Δ+1 colors.
steps: Choose any order of the remaining vertices and maintain colors already assigned.
At a vertex, collect the colors of its already colored neighbors.
Choose a color absent from that set; a palette of Δ+1 always has an available color.
algorithms.proof: At most Δ forbidden neighbor colors exist when any vertex is processed.
algorithms.pitfall: The Δ used in the guarantee is a maximum-degree bound for this remaining graph, not its average degree.

algorithms.name: Random-hyperplane semicoloring
algorithms.label: O(Δ^(log₃2)) semicolors
algorithms.guarantee: In expected polynomial time obtain a sign-pattern labeling with at most n/4 monochromatic edges and O(Δ^(log₃2)) labels. This is a semicoloring, not yet a full proper coloring.
steps: Find unit vectors with adjacent inner products at most −1/2; handle the edgeless case directly.
Choose t=⌈2+log₃Δ⌉ independent standard-Gaussian hyperplane normals and label each vertex by its t projection signs.
Count monochromatic edges. Accept if there are at most n/4; otherwise repeat the random hyperplanes.
algorithms.proof: An edge fails separation in all t planes with probability at most 3^(−t). The expected number of bad edges is small enough for at least constant success probability.
algorithms.pitfall: A sign-pattern label can still contain edges. Never call the output a proper coloring before the deletion step.

algorithms.name: Convert a semicoloring into a full coloring
algorithms.label: O(k log n) full colors
algorithms.guarantee: If each remaining induced graph has a k-label semicoloring with at most one quarter as many bad edges as vertices, repeated extraction yields O(k log n) proper colors.
steps: Run the semicoloring on the current remaining graph.
Discard both endpoints of every monochromatic edge from this round’s selected vertices, retaining at least half the current vertices.
Permanently color those retained vertices by their labels, using fresh colors. Repeat on the discarded vertices until none remain.
algorithms.proof: At most n/2 vertices are deleted per round, and all retained label classes are independent. Geometric decay gives O(log n) rounds.
algorithms.pitfall: Reusing an earlier palette can create conflicts with already colored vertices.

algorithms.name: Vector coloring, hyperplane semicoloring, and degree balancing
algorithms.label: Õ(n^0.38685) colors
algorithms.guarantee: The §6.5 analysis yields Õ(n^(log₆2)) colors; log₆2≈0.38685. Õ suppresses logarithmic factors.
steps: Set σ=n^(log₆3) using the original graph size.
Remove high-degree closed neighborhoods of degree at least σ, using a fresh three-color palette for each.
On the residual maximum-degree-σ graph, use hyperplane semicoloring followed by the full-coloring wrapper.
Balance O(n/σ) neighborhood colors with Õ(σ^(log₃2)) residual colors to get Õ(n^(log₆2)).
algorithms.proof: An edge’s angle is at least 2π/3, so one plane fails to separate it with probability at most 1/3.
algorithms.pitfall: A semicoloring with few bad edges needs a deletion/recursion argument to become a full proper coloring.

algorithms.name: Amplified Gaussian extraction and repeated coloring
algorithms.label: O(Δ^(1/3)√lnΔ · ln n) colors
algorithms.guarantee: Use the independent-set extractor with expected fraction γ=Ω(Δ^(−1/3)/√lnΔ), amplify until a set of size at least γ times the remaining order divided by two is found, and repeatedly remove such sets.
steps: Use a valid lower bound γ from the extractor analysis for the current degree range, with bounded-degree graphs handled greedily.
A single trial yields size at least γn/2 with probability at least γ/2. Run ⌈(2c/γ)ln n⌉ independent trials to make a failed extraction probability at most n^(−c).
Color a successful independent set with one new color and remove it. Recompute on the remaining induced graph and repeat.
Allocate failure probabilities across all extraction rounds; a constant fraction γ/2 removed each round yields O((ln n)/γ) colors.
algorithms.proof: The expected-size statement needs amplification before it can guarantee progress. The geometric removal count and the number of trials per extraction are different quantities.
algorithms.pitfall: Amplification is not merely O(log n) trials independent of γ; its 1/γ dependence is essential.

algorithms.name: Degree balancing for Gaussian coloring
algorithms.label: Õ(n^(1/4)) colors
algorithms.guarantee: The exercise extension balances high-degree neighborhood removal with the Gaussian residual coloring, giving Õ(n^(1/4)) colors.
steps: Set the high-degree threshold D=n^(3/4) using the original graph size.
Repeatedly remove a vertex of degree at least D and its neighborhood, coloring each closed neighborhood with three fresh colors.
Use amplified Gaussian independent-set extraction on the residual graph of maximum degree below D.
Add the two color costs: Õ(n/D+D^(1/3))=Õ(n^(1/4)).
algorithms.proof: The neighborhood removal pays one palette per D deleted vertices, and the residual bound depends on D rather than the original maximum degree.
algorithms.pitfall: This improvement is an explicitly attributed exercise extension, not Theorem 6.24.

problems.title: Large independent set in a 3-colorable graph
problems.input: A promised 3-colorable graph with n vertices and maximum degree Δ.
problems.goal: Extract many pairwise nonadjacent vertices, supplying one color class for the coloring algorithm.
problems.objective: \text{Find a large }I\subseteq V\quad\text{such that}\quad uv\notin E\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in I.

algorithms.name: Gaussian thresholding and deletion of conflicts
algorithms.label: Large expected independent set
algorithms.guarantee: For sufficiently large Δ, the expected set size is Ω(n·Δ^(−1/3)/√lnΔ). Constant-degree cases have elementary greedy alternatives.
steps: Solve the feasible vector program with unit vectors and adjacent inner products exactly −1/2, as in program (13.5).
If Δ≤5, use a greedy (Δ+1)-coloring and return its largest color class. Otherwise set τ=√((2/3)lnΔ).
Draw a standard Gaussian vector r and select S={v:vᵥ·r≥τ}.
Return only vertices of S with no neighbor in S; discard every selected vertex incident to an internal selected edge.
algorithms.proof: Negative correlation on an edge makes adjacent co-selection much rarer than single-vertex selection.
algorithms.pitfall: The selected threshold set can contain edges; the conflict-removal step is essential.

problems.title: Weighted Set Cover
problems.input: A finite universe U, a coverable collection of subsets S, and nonnegative set costs cₛ.
problems.goal: Choose sets whose union is U with minimum total cost.

algorithms.name: Primal–dual tight-set selection
algorithms.label: Factor f
algorithms.guarantee: The output costs at most f·OPT, where f is the maximum number of input sets containing any one element.
steps: Choose an uncovered element e; every set containing e is currently unselected.
Increase only dual variable yₑ by the minimum remaining slack c(S)−Σᵥ∈S yᵥ over sets S containing e.
Select a set attaining this minimum slack, making it tight, and mark all its elements covered. Repeat until the universe is covered.
algorithms.proof: The frequency bound limits repeated charging of one dual variable.
algorithms.pitfall: Frequency per element and cardinality per set are different parameters.

algorithms.name: Greedy cost per newly covered element
algorithms.label: Additional algorithm
algorithms.guarantee: For n=|U|, greedy weighted Set Cover has an Hₙ≤1+ln n approximation guarantee.
steps: At each step, choose a set minimizing its cost divided by the number of uncovered elements it would cover.
Charge its cost equally to those newly covered elements.
Compare the charges within an optimal set and sum the resulting harmonic bound.
algorithms.proof: The denominator must count newly covered elements at the current step.
algorithms.pitfall: Greedy’s logarithmic guarantee and the primal–dual frequency guarantee come from different analyses.

problems.title: Shortest s–t path
problems.input: An undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs and designated vertices s and t.
problems.goal: Find a minimum-total-cost path joining s to t.

algorithms.name: Primal–dual cut growth and path extraction
algorithms.label: Exact algorithm
algorithms.guarantee: The surviving path has cost equal to a feasible dual value, proving optimality.
steps: Start a tree on {s}; its current vertex set S excludes t. Raise the dual variable for the separating cut δ(S) until a crossing edge becomes tight.
Add a tight crossing edge and its outside endpoint to the tree; repeat until t enters the tree.
Return the unique s–t path within the selected tree, discarding all other branches.
algorithms.proof: The returned path crosses each grown tree cut exactly once. Tight path edges charge exactly to the feasible dual, giving equality of primal and dual cost.
algorithms.pitfall: The source’s Algorithm 7.4 extracts the unique tree path. Canonical reverse deletion is the separately taught Steiner-forest cleanup.

problems.title: Generalized Steiner tree / Steiner forest
problems.input: A graph with nonnegative edge costs and prescribed pairs (sᵢ,tᵢ).
problems.goal: Buy minimum-total-cost edges connecting every prescribed pair; different pairs may lie in separate components.
problems.objective: \min_{F\subseteq E}\sum_{e\in F}c_e\quad\text{subject to }s_i,t_i\text{ connected in }(V,F)\text{ for every }i.

algorithms.name: Grow one active component at a time: diagnostic first attempt
algorithms.label: Feasible; displayed dual analysis is insufficient
algorithms.guarantee: The algorithm connects every required pair, but the displayed single-component dual-growth analysis does not establish a constant approximation certificate.
steps: Maintain a forest of tight edges. Choose one connected component that separates some required terminal pair.
Raise that component’s cut dual until a crossing edge becomes tight, add it to the forest, and update components.
Repeat until all pairs are connected; compare its dual accounting with the simultaneous-growth algorithm.
algorithms.proof: Tight crossing edges merge components and ensure feasibility. In the source’s unit-cost example, the primal cost k equals OPT while the generated dual is only one.
algorithms.pitfall: That example defeats this dual certificate; it does not prove that the actual solution is k times worse than OPT.

algorithms.name: Simultaneous moat growth followed by pruning
algorithms.label: Factor 2
algorithms.guarantee: The pruned forest costs at most twice OPT.
steps: Start with isolated vertices and zero cut duals. A component is active exactly when it contains one endpoint but not the other of a required pair.
Raise all active component cut duals at the same rate until an edge becomes tight; add it to the forest and merge components.
When every pair is connected, inspect selected edges in reverse insertion order and delete an edge whenever all prescribed pairs remain connected.
Charge remaining tight edges to active components and use the forest degree bound for the factor-two analysis.
algorithms.proof: The factor two comes from an aggregate forest inequality, not a degree-two bound on every active component.
algorithms.pitfall: Pruning must preserve every demand pair. The source uses reverse insertion order; arbitrary-order deletion is a valid separately attributed Exercise 7.4 extension.

problems.title: Probabilistic approximation by tree metrics
problems.input: A finite metric d on n points, with positive distances rescaled when needed.
problems.goal: Construct a distribution of dominating tree metrics with logarithmic expected pairwise stretch.
problems.objective: d(u,v)\le d_T(u,v)\quad\text{for every sample},\qquad\mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le O(\log n)\,d(u,v).

algorithms.name: Random hierarchical metric decomposition
algorithms.label: Expected O(log n) stretch
algorithms.guarantee: Every sampled tree dominates original distances; each fixed pair has expected stretch O(log n).
steps: Rescale the metric if needed and choose a top scale Δ that is a power of two greater than twice the diameter. Draw one uniform permutation π of all vertices and one r₀ uniformly from [1/2,1).

At scale i set rᵢ=2ⁱr₀. Within each current parent cluster, assign unassigned points to the first radius-rᵢ ball centered at π(j) that contains them; centers range over the entire original vertex set.
Repeat at decreasing scales until singleton leaves. Connect each cluster to its parent with the source’s scale edge length 2ⁱ.
Use the resulting hierarchical tree metric: each sample dominates original distances, and a fixed pair has expected tree distance O(log n) times its original distance.
algorithms.proof: Random separation probabilities control each pair’s expected distortion even though some sampled pairs can be highly stretched.
algorithms.pitfall: This is a metric construction guarantee, not a claim that one tree simultaneously has logarithmic worst-case stretch for all pairs.

problems.title: Buy-at-bulk network design
problems.input: Edge lengths ℓₑ, terminal-pair demands dᵢ, and a common nondecreasing capacity cost f with f(0)=0 and f(u)/u nonincreasing for positive u (economies of scale).
problems.goal: Choose a route for each demand and enough edge capacity, minimizing total installation cost.

algorithms.name: Exact buy-at-bulk routing on a tree
algorithms.label: Exact on a supplied tree
algorithms.guarantee: A tree has only one path per demand pair. Routing each demand on that path and installing exactly the resulting load is optimal for every nondecreasing edge installation function.
steps: For each source–sink pair find its unique tree path and send the entire prescribed demand along it.
For each tree edge, sum all demands whose paths contain that edge.
Install exactly that capacity and pay the edge’s installation cost at that load.
algorithms.proof: Every feasible route must cross the same tree edges; nondecreasing cost means extra capacity cannot improve the objective.
algorithms.pitfall: The exact guarantee is for the tree instance, not the original general metric.

algorithms.name: Remove auxiliary vertices from the sampled hierarchical tree
algorithms.label: Distances increase by at most factor 4
algorithms.guarantee: For the source’s hierarchical tree with the original vertices as leaves, contraction yields a tree on original vertices with Tᵤᵥ≤T′ᵤᵥ≤4Tᵤᵥ.
steps: Start with the hierarchical tree produced by the embedding, whose original metric vertices label leaves.
Repeatedly contract an edge from a labeled vertex into an unlabeled parent, preserving the original labels and continuing until all auxiliary vertices are removed.
Multiply the remaining edge lengths by four. Use the hierarchy’s geometric scales to compare all original pair distances.
algorithms.proof: Geometric level lengths bound the distortion caused by label-preserving contractions; the final scaling restores domination.
algorithms.pitfall: This factor-four statement is specific to the hierarchical tree in the source, not an arbitrary tree contraction.

algorithms.name: Route on a random tree and transfer to the graph
algorithms.label: Expected O(log n) approximation
algorithms.guarantee: The construction gives an expected O(log n) approximation under the stated economies-of-scale assumptions.
steps: Take the graph’s shortest-path metric and sample a dominating tree metric. Convert to a tree on the original vertices using the source’s constant-distortion transformation.
Route each demand on its unique tree path, buying the sum of the demands using each tree edge.
Replace tree edges by corresponding shortest paths in the original graph and merge capacities where routes share graph edges.
Compare with a fixed optimum: expected metric stretch bounds transferred length, and subadditivity of f bounds merged-capacity cost.
algorithms.proof: Economies of scale imply subadditivity. Pairwise expected stretch is enough after summing the fixed optimum’s cost.
algorithms.pitfall: Replacing the general capacity cost by a linear function treats only a special case and removes the bulk-discount behavior.

problems.title: Maximum-weight independent set in planar graphs
problems.input: A planar graph with nonnegative vertex weights and a planar embedding, obtained by a standard polynomial-time embedding routine if needed.
problems.goal: Find an independent set of maximum total vertex weight approximately; cardinality is the special case of unit weights.

algorithms.name: Weighted independent-set DP on a rooted tree
algorithms.label: Exact; linear tree time
algorithms.guarantee: For a tree with nonnegative vertex weights, a two-state dynamic program returns a maximum-weight independent set in linear time.
steps: Root the tree and process children before their parent.
Use IN(u)=wᵤ+Σchild OUT(child), and OUT(u)=Σchild max{IN(child),OUT(child)}.
At the root take the better state and reconstruct choices, forcing children out whenever their parent is included.
algorithms.proof: Distinct child subtrees interact only through their parent. The two states encode its entire effect.
algorithms.pitfall: This recurrence depends on the tree structure; applying it directly to a cyclic graph omits conflicts.

algorithms.name: Weighted independent set on a supplied tree decomposition
algorithms.label: Exact; O(2^O(t)N)
algorithms.guarantee: Given a valid width-t decomposition with N bags, solve weighted independent set by compatible bag subsets in O(2^O(t)N) time.
steps: Root the bag tree. For every bag list its independent vertex subsets as possible states.
For a fixed parent state, maximize each child contribution over child states that agree on the shared bag intersection.
Subtract the shared selected-vertex weight when combining subproblem values so that no vertex is charged twice.
Choose the best root state and use stored maximizing states to reconstruct the independent set.
algorithms.proof: The running-intersection property separates child subgraphs once the selected vertices of the bag are fixed.
algorithms.pitfall: Bag membership alone is insufficient: a valid tree decomposition must satisfy edge coverage and connected occurrence of every vertex.

algorithms.name: Construct the bounded-width outerplanar decomposition
algorithms.label: Width O(k); exact k-outerplanar solver
algorithms.guarantee: The source constructs a width-O(k) decomposition of a k-outerplanar graph and combines it with bag DP for O(2^O(k)n²) weighted independent-set time.
steps: Use the planar embedding to split high-degree vertices into a degree-at-most-three expansion, preserving a mapping back to original vertices for the decomposition.
Recursively remove exterior-face edges, construct a spanning forest of the remainder, then extend it by exterior edges without cycles; the resulting forest has fundamental-cycle load at most 3k.
Create vertex and forest-edge bags. For every nonforest edge propagate one endpoint along the bags of its fundamental forest path, giving width at most the load plus one.
Map split-vertex bag occurrences back to original vertices and run the weighted bag-state DP on the resulting decomposition.
algorithms.proof: Bounded outerplanarity controls fundamental-cycle load, which controls bag width. The split graph is only a tool for constructing bags.
algorithms.pitfall: Do not solve MIS on the split graph as if its independent sets were the original independent sets.

algorithms.name: Baker’s layer deletion and bounded-treewidth DP
algorithms.label: PTAS
algorithms.guarantee: For fixed 0<ε<1, return an independent set of weight at least (1−ε)OPT in polynomial time. The exact k-outerplanar subroutine runs in O(2^O(k)n²).
steps: Assign successive outer-face layers of the planar embedding. Choose k with 1/k≤ε.
For every residue modulo k, delete that class of layers. Every remaining component has bounded outerplanarity O(k).
Construct its bounded-width tree decomposition and run the exact weighted bag-state independent-set DP.
Return the heaviest result over all residues. Averaging the weight of a fixed optimum over layer classes bounds the lost weight by OPT/k.
algorithms.proof: Averaging limits the lost optimum; bounded treewidth supplies the exact subroutine on what remains.
algorithms.pitfall: The treewidth bound depends on the layered planar structure; arbitrary vertex deletion does not provide it.

problems.title: Three-variable odd/even constraint satisfaction
problems.input: A collection of odd/even parity constraints, each on three distinct Boolean variables; nonnegative weights can be summed in the same way.
problems.goal: Find an assignment maximizing the total satisfied constraint weight.

algorithms.name: Choose the better of the two constant assignments
algorithms.label: Deterministic factor 1/2
algorithms.guarantee: All-one satisfies every odd constraint, and all-zero satisfies every even constraint. Their better value is at least half the total weight and hence at least OPT/2.
steps: Evaluate the total satisfied weight for the assignment setting every variable to zero.
Evaluate the total satisfied weight for the assignment setting every variable to one.
Return whichever complete assignment has the larger satisfied weight.
algorithms.proof: Each three-variable odd/even constraint is satisfied by exactly one of the two constant assignments. Their values sum to total constraint weight.
algorithms.pitfall: The argument uses odd arity. For even-arity parity constraints, the two constant assignments need not complement one another.

problems.title: Metric traveling salesman problem
problems.input: A complete undirected graph with nonnegative symmetric edge costs satisfying the triangle inequality.
problems.goal: Find a minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex exactly once.

algorithms.name: Christofides’ algorithm
algorithms.label: Factor 3/2
algorithms.guarantee: The tour costs at most 3OPT/2 for metric symmetric TSP.
steps: Compute a minimum spanning tree and its even-sized set of odd-degree vertices.
Find a minimum-cost perfect matching on those odd-degree vertices and add it to the tree.
Take an Euler tour of the resulting connected even-degree multigraph, then shortcut repeated vertices.
algorithms.proof: The MST costs at most OPT, the matching at most OPT/2, and metric shortcutting does not increase length.
algorithms.pitfall: The guarantee relies on symmetry and the triangle inequality.

problems.title: Euclidean traveling salesman problem
problems.input: A set of points in the Euclidean plane.
problems.goal: Find a shortest Euclidean tour through all points.

algorithms.name: Geometric dissection, portals, and dynamic programming
algorithms.label: PTAS
algorithms.guarantee: For fixed ε>0, Euclidean TSP in the plane admits a randomized (1+ε) approximation in n·(log n)^{O(1/ε)} time, with success probability at least 1/2 per random dissection; all polynomially many integer shifts may be enumerated.
steps: Snap and scale to a nice instance, keeping the two-way tour-length perturbation explicit.
Randomly shift a recursive square dissection; place nested portals on each side.
Use the crossing/patching structure theorem: m=O(log n/ε) portals per side and r=O(1/ε) crossings suffice with probability at least 1/2.
Dynamic-program over squares, boundary portal occurrences and entry/exit pairings; merge four children without creating premature cycles.
Shortcut portal visits by the Euclidean triangle inequality, undo snapping and allocate accuracy across the reductions.
algorithms.proof: If each point moves by at most δ, each edge changes by at most 2δ and any n-edge tour by at most 2nδ. Applying this once to the old optimum and once to the returned tour gives C≤(1+η)OPT+(2+η)2nδ. A boundary state must record portal occurrences with multiplicity and which entry is paired with which exit. Four boundary points can have identical used portals but different connections, so a portal subset alone is insufficient. The structural theorem is the hard geometric input. Random shift makes scale-specific patching and portal detours cheap in expectation. With expected overhead ≤ηOPT/2, Markov gives overhead ≤ηOPT with probability ≥1/2. With m=O(log n/η) and r=O(1/η), the DP costs m^{O(r)}n log n, absorbed into n(log n)^{O(1/η)} for fixed η. The weaker r=O(m) bound only yields n^{O(log log n)}. For each state enumerate compatible internal crossings and pairings of four child squares, reject inconsistent connections and closed subtours that leave points outside, then minimize the sum of child costs. At the root require one closed tour. Independent repetition t times reduces structural failure to at most 2^(−t); taking the best feasible output never worsens cost. Enumerating all O(n²) shifts of a nice instance also finds a good shift.
algorithms.pitfall: Two partial solutions can use the same four portals but pair them as (a,b),(c,d) or (a,c),(b,d). Only one may connect to the outside without a premature cycle. Record multiplicity and connectivity.

problems.title: Weighted Vertex Cover
problems.input: An undirected graph and nonnegative vertex costs wᵥ.
problems.goal: Choose a minimum-weight set containing at least one endpoint of every edge.
problems.objective: \min_{C\subseteq V}\sum_{v\in C}w_v\quad\text{subject to}\quad C\cap\{u,v\}\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }uv\in E.

algorithms.name: Threshold rounding of the covering LP
algorithms.label: Factor 2
algorithms.guarantee: Selecting all vertices with LP value at least 1/2 gives a feasible cover of cost at most twice OPT.
steps: Solve the LP minimizing weighted vertex values subject to xᵤ+xᵥ≥1 on every edge.
Select every vertex whose fractional value is at least 1/2, including equality.
Each edge has a selected endpoint, and the selected indicator is at most twice the fractional value for every vertex.
algorithms.proof: Feasibility and the objective bound follow from two pointwise inequalities.
algorithms.pitfall: Using a strict threshold greater than 1/2 can leave an edge with two half-valued endpoints uncovered.

sectionAudit.tool: Nice-instance reduction, random dissection, portals, patching lemma and connectivity-aware dynamic programming.

hardnessConstructions.title: PARTITION to bin packing
hardnessConstructions.construction: Scale integers bᵢ summing to B into sizes 2bᵢ/B. A partition packs in two bins; absence of a partition needs at least three. Items larger than one immediately certify NO.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: This rules out an absolute factor below 3/2 unless P=NP; it does not rule out an additive-bin APTAS.

hardnessConstructions.title: Hypothetical FPTAS to an exact algorithm
hardnessConstructions.construction: If integer OPT has a polynomial upper bound nq(n), choose ε≤1/(2nq(n)). An assumed FPTAS then returns an integer value less than OPT+1, forcing equality.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: This is a contradiction wrapper for strong NP-hardness, not a constructed FPTAS.

hardnessConstructions.title: 3-dimensional matching to threshold-three scheduling
hardnessConstructions.construction: Create one machine for each triple, unit-time element jobs allowed only on incident triples, and m−n dummy jobs of length three. A schedule of makespan at most three exists exactly for a perfect matching.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: This first construction proves feasibility hardness; use the refined threshold-two gadget for the strict 3/2 approximation gap.

hardnessConstructions.title: Refined restricted-assignment scheduling gap
hardnessConstructions.construction: Create unit jobs for the B and C elements. For each a, create kₐ−1 length-two dummy jobs allowed on its type-a triple machines. Deal with absent a-elements as immediate NO cases.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: YES has OPT≤2 and NO has integer OPT≥3, excluding factors below 3/2 unless P=NP.

hardnessConstructions.title: Directed edge-disjoint-path gap amplification
hardnessConstructions.construction: Arrange k pair-routes and replace their crossings by copies of the hard two-pair directed routing instance. Select k as a polynomial in the base arc count for fixed ε.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: YES routes all k pairs; NO routes at most one. Track the O(k²|A|) new arc count before expressing the hardness exponent.

hardnessConstructions.title: Earlier reductions recapped in the assigned section
hardnessConstructions.construction: Review the dominating-set to {1,2}-distance k-center gap, Hamiltonian-cycle to nonmetric-TSP cost gap, and PARTITION to two-versus-three-bin gap.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: These are recaps of earlier reductions. They do not make every positive algorithm in those earlier chapters assigned.

hardnessConstructions.title: PCP verifier to a bounded-arity gap CSP
hardnessConstructions.construction: Enumerate polynomially many random tapes, create one local acceptance predicate per tape, and share one Boolean variable for each global proof location.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: Completeness c and soundness s exclude a maximization fraction greater than s/c. The PCP theorem is an input.

hardnessConstructions.title: Odd/even PCP to parity CSP
hardnessConstructions.construction: Translate each three-query parity test into its odd or even constraint, keeping the common global proof variables.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: Retain YES≥1−ε and NO≤1/2+δ through the ratio comparison; pair it with the positive half-approximation story.

hardnessConstructions.title: Four-clause parity to MAX-E3SAT gadget
hardnessConstructions.construction: For each three-variable parity predicate, introduce the four three-literal clauses that exclude exactly its four violating assignments.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: A satisfied parity yields four satisfied clauses, otherwise three. Direct gap accounting gives the sharp 7/8 barrier; the coarser L-reduction analysis yields 13/14.

hardnessConstructions.title: Direct OR-PCP to MAX-E3SAT
hardnessConstructions.construction: Use the OR-of-three-literals acceptance tests themselves as the clauses, sharing global proof-bit variables across random tapes.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: Completeness one and soundness 7/8+δ are imported from the PCP theorem, not derived by merely enumerating clauses.

hardnessConstructions.title: Twelve-clause parity to MAX-2SAT gadget
hardnessConstructions.construction: Use the source’s twelve-clause even-parity gadget with four fresh auxiliary variables per constraint; flip one original literal for odd parity. Optimize auxiliary choices locally.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: Satisfied parity permits eleven clauses and violated parity at most ten; the resulting limiting ratio is 21/22, not 7/8.

hardnessConstructions.title: Clique and independent set by complementation
hardnessConstructions.construction: Complement the general graph, preserve vertex weights, and use the same selected set: cliques become independent sets and conversely.
hardnessConstructions.lesson: The transformation does not preserve planarity; it cannot transfer arbitrary-graph hardness to the planar PTAS.
